title: Ming Great Wall
summary: Between 1368 and 1644 the Ming dynasty built an 8,852 km frontier line of walls, trenches, towers and passes from Liaoning to Gansu, mostly in surges driven by Mongol raids; its brick-faced eastern sections are the Great Wall most people picture.
card: The Ming at first held the northern frontier with forts and passes, and only from 1437 joined them with continuous wall. Building peaked between 1465 and 1566 as Mongol raids grew, and after Altan Khan broke through near Gubeikou in 1550, Qi Jiguang lined the wall near Beijing with about 1,200 hollow brick towers. China's 2012 survey measures the Ming line at 8,851.8 km, including trenches and natural barriers.
what:
The Ming Great Wall is the frontier line built by the Ming dynasty (1368–1644) across northern China, and the wall most visitors picture. China's 2012 survey measured it at 8,851.8 km: 6,259.6 km of built wall, 359.7 km of trench and 2,232.5 km of ridges, rivers and other natural barriers worked into the line, with 17,449 towers and other single structures and 1,272 passes and forts. The main line runs from Hushan in eastern Liaoning to Jiayuguan in Gansu.

It was never one project. A 2024 study combining Ming records, field survey and GIS divides it into five phases. Under the first emperors (1368–1435) the frontier was held by 453 forts and passes, among them Jiayuguan (1372) and Shanhaiguan (1381), and no continuous wall. The first continuous wall rose in Liaodong between 1437 and 1442. After the Ming army's defeat by the Mongols at Tumu in 1449 the court moved from attack to defence, and between 1465 and 1521 the frontier districts built about 5,400 km of wall; Badaling's fort dates from 1505. A second surge came under the Jiajing emperor (1522–1566), when Mongol raids were heaviest: about 1,340 km of new wall and 3,780 km of rebuilding, including the whole Jizhou line near Beijing in 1551. In 1550 Altan Khan's cavalry broke through near Gubeikou and plundered the countryside around Beijing for three days. From 1568 Qi Jiguang rebuilt the Jizhou wall with hollow brick towers, about 1,200 of them, finished in 1571. After a peace with Altan Khan in the Longqing reign, building slowed; the last new walls went up in the north-west, and Liaodong repaired 1,050 km of wall in 1608 against the rising Jurchens. In 1644 the Qing army entered through Shanhaiguan and the Ming fell.

Figures differ by method. ICOMOS in 1987 gave 5,650 km of crenellated wall with 25,000 towers; the survey's larger total counts trenches, branch lines and natural barriers.

uncertainty.note: Bounded by the dynasty. Continuous wall-building began in 1437; Yang et al. (2024) find no large-scale construction after 1620, hence the end_minus range.

how: The Ming built forts, passes and beacon piers first and only later joined them with wall. In the east the wall is a core of rubble and loess faced with brick and dressed stone, or built entirely of stone, with a walkway and crenellations; in the west it is mostly rammed earth. The line belonged to a layered system: nine, later eleven, frontier military districts (Zhenbao and Chang were added to protect the capital and the imperial tombs), about 1,100 garrisons ranked in five levels (zhen, lu, wei, suo, bao), and thousands of posts, beacon towers and relay stations. Construction was organised by district and assigned to garrison troops section by section. When Qi Jiguang took over Jizhou in 1568 he argued that walls repaired every year simply fell down again, and proposed towers straddling the wall, 5 zhang tall, hollow, in three storeys, each holding 100 men with armour, weapons and grain; he asked for 1,200 to be built first and, finding the frontier troops undisciplined, brought in soldiers from Zhejiang. The towers were finished in the autumn of 1571. At Zhuizi Mountain on the Liaoning–Hebei border, a section first built in 1381, the surviving wall is 1.5–4.3 m wide and up to 9.8 m high.
why_it_matters: The Ming wall is the Great Wall of popular imagination: its brick towers on the ridges north of Beijing, at Badaling, Mutianyu and Jinshanling, shape how the world pictures China's past, and Badaling alone drew more than 76.5 million visitors between 2005 and 2015. Historically it records two centuries of conflict with the Mongols. Its building surges track the raids, and it did not always hold: in 1550 Altan Khan's riders broke through near Gubeikou and plundered the capital region for three days, and in 1567 his forces killed tens of thousands of people in Shanxi. Peace came by negotiation rather than masonry, when the Longqing court enfeoffed Altan Khan and opened border markets. In 1644 Shanhaiguan, which earlier Later Jin incursions had bypassed, was opened to the Qing army, and the Ming fell. Without the Jiajing-era surge and Qi Jiguang's towers there would be no brick-towered wall around Beijing; Ming defence would have rested on the scattered forts of the early dynasty. Today the Ming wall is also a conservation problem: only about 5.8% of its length is well preserved, and over half has vanished or decayed badly.

perspectives.account: The Ming wall was built in five phases between 1368 and 1620, forts and passes first and continuous wall later, and each surge followed the intensity of warfare with the Mongols.

perspectives.holder: Qi Jiguang, memorial recorded in Ming Shi 212
perspectives.account: Repairing the Jizhou wall every year was wasted effort because it kept collapsing; defence needed garrisoned towers along the wall and properly trained troops.

perspectives.holder: Wang Chonggu, memorial recorded in Ming Shi 327
perspectives.account: Granting Altan Khan a title and tribute trade would buy years of peace in which the frontier could be strengthened, which was better than endless defensive scrambling; the court accepted this in the Longqing reign.
The Ming built 5,650 km of crenellated wall fortified by 25,000 towers and 15,000 outposts, figures that predate and differ from the 2012 survey's 8,851.8 km.
